operations.title: Gmail message received
operations.setup: In YOUR app's Google Cloud project (the one owning the OAuth client): create a Pub/Sub topic, grant publish on it to gmail-api-push@system.gserviceaccount.com, and create a PUSH subscription to the route your host mounts for this trigger, with authentication on (a service account you choose; the endpoint URL as the audience). Put that audience and service account on the connection as pushAudience and pushServiceAccount, and fetch Google's signing keys for verification. Then call mailbox_watch with the topic for each mailbox and store its historyId as the trigger's cursor (startHistoryId); renew the watch daily. ONE topic serves every mailbox: route each push by its emailAddress, and only after the token verifies, to a mailbox you watched; drop an unmapped address with a 2xx. Persist cursor.next when a run succeeds. On cursor-expired or cursor-overflow, watch again for a fresh historyId FIRST, then list with message_list using the resyncQuery, and match it against the mail you already handled. This trigger never changes read state.

operations.title: Google Calendar change
operations.setup: The host mints a UUID, calls channel_watch with it, its own URL for this trigger and the connection's channelToken, and stores the returned id, resourceId and expiration. The first message on a new channel is `sync` and carries no change.

operations.title: HubSpot CRM event
operations.setup: In the HubSpot app's webhook settings, set the target URL to the route your host mounts for this trigger and subscribe to the deal, contact and company events you want. Deliveries are signed with the app's client secret, already on the connection as `clientSecret`. ONE URL serves every portal that installed the app, so route each event by its portalId, and only after the signature has verified: map portalId to the connection created when that portal installed, and drop an unmapped portalId with a 2xx and a log line, creating nothing. HubSpot retries a failed delivery, and eventId is not guaranteed to be unique, so never dedupe on eventId alone: a retry is the same event resent, differing only in attemptNumber, so compare every other field. operations.title: Outlook calendar change
operations.setup: The host calls subscription_create with its own URL for this trigger, an expiry of now plus this lifetime, and the connection's clientState, and must answer Graph's validationToken challenge on that URL as plain text within 10 seconds or the subscription is refused. It stores the returned id and expirationDateTime. 3600 seconds before expiry it calls subscription_renew; a 404 there means the subscription is gone and it re-lists (event_list) and creates again, because notifications during the gap are gone. Every notification is a batch: the host compares each item's clientState with the connection's clientState, answers 202, and then processes the items. A `missed` lifecycle event means re-list; `reauthorizationRequired` means renew; `subscriptionRemoved` means create again and re-list.

credentials.label: Access token
credentials.help: From the Square developer dashboard. SANDBOX and PRODUCTION tokens are different values for different hosts -- a sandbox token is refused by the production host rather than accepted, which is the whole reason this provider's estates cannot be confused.

sandbox.warning: A separate test host. Selecting sandbox mode changes the base URL.
sandbox.note: The one sandbox kind that is genuinely a DIFFERENT PLACE. Stripe's estate is chosen by the key, Telegram's and HubSpot's by the account, SES's not at all -- Square's is another host, with its own data and its own credentials. A sandbox access token sent to the production host is refused rather than silently reaching the real ledger, which makes this the SAFEST of the four kinds and worth saying so: the failure mode is a 401, not a charge.

connectors.idempotencyNote: Square takes the key in the BODY, not in a header, and lists it as REQUIRED. Every provider before this one that supported idempotency used a header, so the generator had exactly one place to put a key. The distinction is not cosmetic: it is the difference between a retried durable run charging once and charging twice.

credentials.label: Secret key
credentials.help: sk_test_... for the test estate, sk_live_... for the real ledger. The key -- not the URL -- decides which one you reach.

credentials.label: Webhook signing secret
credentials.help: whsec_... from the endpoint you added in the Stripe dashboard. Required only by the webhook trigger.

sandbox.warning: The KEY decides live-or-test, not the endpoint — the same host serves both. A live key pointed at a node marked “sandbox” reaches the real estate and SUCCEEDS. Nothing in the request distinguishes them, which is why the credential sits on the connection.
sandbox.note: Stripe's test estate is selected by the KEY, not the URL -- api.stripe.com serves both. A live key sent to a node whose mode says "sandbox" reaches the real ledger and succeeds. Nothing in the request distinguishes them, which is exactly why credentials sit on the connection rather than on twelve separate nodes.

connectors.idempotencyNote: Retried durable runs MUST not create a second charge. This header is what makes `unsafe-to-replay` recoverable rather than merely forbidden.

operations.title: Stripe event
operations.setup: Add an endpoint in the Stripe dashboard (or via POST /v1/webhook_endpoints) pointing at the route your host mounts for this trigger, then put the endpoint's signing secret on the connection as `webhookSecret`.

credentials.label: Bot token
credentials.help: From @BotFather — 123456:ABC-DEF… . A bot registered in the test environment is a DIFFERENT bot with a different token; the same token does not reach both.

sandbox.warning: A test estate on the same host, reached with credentials from a separate test account somebody has to register first.
sandbox.note: Telegram's test environment is a genuinely SEPARATE ACCOUNT: you create a new account inside it and register a new bot there, so the sandbox credential is a different token rather than the same one pointed elsewhere. The `/test` path segment is how you reach it; the account is what makes it separate. Flood limits are NOT relaxed there, so it is a place to test, not a place to hammer.

operations.title: Telegram message
operations.setup: The host polls getUpdates on a schedule and persists the `offset` cursor between calls, passing the last `cursor` back in — Telegram queues nothing once an offset has acknowledged it, so a lost cursor is lost updates. getUpdates and setWebhook are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE for one bot: a host running both gets neither.

connectors.summary: Send SMS with Twilio from a workflow or a Laravel app, and read a message's delivery status.

credentials.label: Account SID
credentials.help: AC followed by 32 hex characters, from the Twilio Console. It is part of every request URL.

credentials.label: API key SID (or Account SID)
credentials.help: An API key SID from the Twilio Console (API keys & tokens), recommended. Or the Account SID again, to authenticate with the Auth Token.

credentials.label: API key secret (or Auth Token)
credentials.help: The secret shown once when the API key was created, or the account's Auth Token. The Auth Token can do everything on the account; an API key can be revoked on its own.

sandbox.warning: The KEY decides live-or-test, not the endpoint — the same host serves both. A live key pointed at a node marked “sandbox” reaches the real estate and SUCCEEDS. Nothing in the request distinguishes them, which is why the credential sits on the connection.
sandbox.note: Twilio's test estate is selected by the CREDENTIALS, not the URL: a separate test Account SID and test Auth Token (Console -> API keys & tokens), against the same api.twilio.com. A live key on a node marked sandbox texts a real phone and is billed. With test credentials only message_send works -- every other resource, including message_get, answers 403 -- nothing is sent or charged, no status callback fires, and From must be Twilio's magic +15005550006 (+15005550004 as To returns 21610, the STOP case). Test credentials are the test Account SID and Auth Token, not an API key.

setup.title: Find your Account SID
setup.detail: Sign in to the Twilio Console; the Account SID is on the Console home page. It is AC followed by 32 hex characters, and it is part of every URL this connector calls. A TRIAL account can only send to verified numbers (up to 5; your sign-up number is verified already), so upgrade before sending to anyone else.

setup.title: Create a Standard API key for {{appName}}
setup.detail: Console: Settings, Account settings, API keys & auth tokens, then Create API key. Choose Standard: it reaches every API this connector uses, but not the Accounts or Keys resources, so it cannot create more keys if it leaks. Copy the key's SID into the username and its secret into the password, and store the secret immediately. Leave the region at the default unless your account uses another Twilio region: this connector calls api.twilio.com.

setup.title: Give {{appName}} a sender
setup.detail: Either a Twilio phone number with SMS capability, or a Messaging Service (Console: Messaging, Services, Create Messaging Service, then add your numbers to its sender pool). message_send takes one of From or MessagingServiceSid; for Laravel notifications set TWILIO_FROM or TWILIO_MESSAGING_SERVICE_SID so a notification that names no sender still has one.

setup.title: Register for A2P 10DLC before texting US numbers
setup.detail: Anyone sending application SMS to the US from a 10-digit long code must register for A2P 10DLC, hobbyists included, and unregistered traffic incurs additional carrier fees. If the number only sends verification codes, Twilio Verify can be used instead of registering.

setup.title: Send a test message and read it back
setup.detail: Send one SMS to a phone you can read, then read it back with message_get to see what Twilio did with it.
setup.prompt: Using {{appName}}'s {{connector}} connection, send one SMS with message_send to a phone the person can read (on a trial account, a verified number), then call message_get with the returned sid and report its status, error_code and error_message.
setup.done: message_get reports status sent or delivered with error_code null, and the person received the text.

credentials.help: From Google Cloud Console. One value for the whole installation.

credentials.label: OAuth client secret
credentials.help: The client secret for the same OAuth app.

credentials.help: Per connected YouTube account; expires after one hour.

credentials.label: Refresh token
credentials.help: Per connected YouTube account; the host uses it to refresh the access token.

sandbox.warning: No test estate, and somebody checked. Everything this connector does is real. Use the faker.

credentials.label: OAuth client ID
credentials.help: From the Zoom app you registered at marketplace.zoom.us. One value for the whole installation -- the same app serves every connected Zoom account.

credentials.label: OAuth client secret
credentials.help: From the same app. Used to exchange the code and to refresh; never sent with an API request.

credentials.label: Access token
credentials.help: Obtained by the host's OAuth exchange, PER CONNECTED ZOOM ACCOUNT. Expires after one hour -- a host that does not refresh will work for a while and then fail with no warning.

credentials.label: Refresh token
credentials.help: Also per account. A NEW one is issued on every refresh -- persist the replacement atomically, and never retry a refresh that may have already succeeded: replaying an old refresh token is Zoom's own reported failure mode for a rotating grant.

sandbox.warning: NOBODY HAS CHECKED whether a test estate exists. Not the same as “no”. Treat every call as real.
sandbox.note: Zoom has no test estate distinct from a real account, as far as this review found (2026-09-15) -- but it is UNVERIFIED, not confirmed. Every call authorizes against the caller's own Zoom account and can read real meeting data. Use fake mode while building.
